14                                                                            
   v.                                   FAITH SETTLEMENT                     
15                                                                            
   SUZY CLEANERS, an organization, et al.,                                   
                                        [Doc. 147]                           
16                                                                            
                           Defendants.                                       
17                                                                            
18                                                                            
19       Plaintiff  Pacific  Resources  Associates  LLC  (“Plaintiff”)  previously  owned  a 
20  storefront in the Valley Plaza shopping center in Escondido, California.  Plaintiff seeks 
21  relief against the current and former owners and operators of two separate dry-cleaning 
22  businesses located in the same shopping center for allegedly contaminating the soil beneath 
23  its property with perchloroethylene (“PCE”), a chlorinated solvent commonly used in the 
24  dry-cleaning industry.                                                    
25       Defendant  M&E  Brothers,  LLC  (“M&E”)  has  reached  a  tentative  settlement 
26  agreement with Plaintiff and now moves this Court to approve the settlement as made in 
27  “good faith” in accordance with California Code of Civil Procedure sections 877 and 877.6 
28  on the grounds that the settlement agreement between Plaintiff and M&E meets the test for 
1  “good faith” set forth in Tech-Bilt, Inc. v. Woodward-Clyde & Associates, 38 Cal.3d 488 
2  (1985) (“Motion”).  (Doc. 147.)  Additionally, M&E seeks an order barring all existing and 
3  future claims against it for indemnity and/or contribution.  (Id.)  Plaintiff joined M&E’s 
4  Motion.  (Doc. 149.)                                                      
5       Defendants Kim Hortman Buhler (as administrator and executor of the Estate of 
6  Barbara Hortman) and Kim Hortman Buhler and Norman Alton Hortman III (as trustees 
7  of The Norman Alton Hortman and Barbara Hortman Revocable Trust No. 1 Dated July 2, 
8  1985) (collectively, the “Hortmans”) oppose  M&E’s Motion on the grounds that  the 
9  indemnity/contribution bar requested by M&E is overbroad (the “Hortman Opposition”).  
10  (Doc. 158.)                                                               
11       Defendants Guhn Y. Kim, Yun Soon Kim, and The Kim Family Trust of 2017 
12  (collectively, the “Kims”) also oppose the M&E’s Motion on the grounds that the proposed 
13  settlement is disproportionate to M&E’s estimated liability.  Like the Hortmans, the Kims 
14  also  contend  that  the  requested  indemnity/contribution  bar  is  overbroad  (the  “Kim 
15  Opposition”).  (Doc. 157.)                                                
16       On August 21, 2023, M&E filed its Reply in Support of its Motion for Good Faith 
17  Settlement against the Hortmans (the “Hortman Reply”).  (Doc. 162.)  The same day, M&E 
18  filed its Reply in Support of its Motion for Good Faith Settlement against the Kims (the 
19  “Kim Reply”).  (Doc. 163.)                                                
20       After careful consideration, the Court GRANTS M&E’s Motion but clarifies the 
21  permissible scope of the requested contribution/indemnity bar.            
22                           I.   BACKGROUND                                  
23  A.   Statement of Facts                                                   
24       1.   Plaintiff and the 1680 Property                                 
25       Plaintiff owned  the property located at 1680 East Valley Parkway, Escondido, 
26  California 92027, a storefront in the Valley Plaza shopping center, from February 12, 2001 
27  until November 2022 (the “1680 Property”).  (Doc. 114, Second Amended Complaint 
28  (“SAC”), ¶ 33.)                                                           
1       2.   M&E, the Hortmans, and the 1718 Property                        
2       M&E owns the property located at 1718 East Valley Parkway, Escondido, California 
3  92027, another storefront in the Valley Plaza shopping center (the “1718 Property”).  (Doc. 
4  147 at 7.)1  The 1718 Property is located east of Plaintiff’s 1680 Property.  (Doc. 153 at 4.)  
5  Prior to M&E’s ownership, the 1718 Property was home to a dry-cleaning business owned 
6  and operated by the Hortmans.  (Declaration of Flor De Lys Barawid (“Barawid Decl.”) 
7  ¶ 8 [Doc. 147-8].)                                                        
8       3.   The Kims and the 1654 Property                                  
9       The Kims own  the property located at 1654  East Valley  Parkway,  Escondido, 
10  California  92027,  a  third  storefront  in  the  Valley  Plaza  shopping  center  (the  “1654 
11  Property”).  (Doc. 147 at 9.)  The 1654 Property is located west of Plaintiff’s 1680 Property.  
12  (Doc. 153 at 4.)  The 1654 Property is currently home to Suzy Cleaners.  (Doc. 157 at 12.)  
13       4.   Plaintiff’s Allegations                                         
14       In its SAC, Plaintiff alleges that all former and current owners and operators of the 
15  dry-cleaning businesses located at the 1654 Property and the 1718 Property (including the 
16  Kims and the Hortmans) released PCE into the soil beneath the properties, which then 
17  migrated and contaminated the soil beneath Plaintiff’s 1680 Property.  (SAC ¶¶ 36, 39, 41.)  
18  Plaintiff alleges that it has incurred substantial response costs and will continue to incur 
19  response, removal, and remediation costs in the future.  (SAC ¶¶ 40, 42–46.)  Notably, 
20  however, Plaintiff no longer owns the 1680 Property.  (SAC ¶ 33.)         
21  B.   Procedural History                                                   
22       Plaintiff initially filed this case on February 6, 2020—nearly four years ago.  (Doc. 
23  1.)  Plaintiff then amended its complaint on February 3, 2023 (Doc. 83) and on May 1, 
24  2023  (Doc.  114).    Plaintiff’s  SAC  asserts  three  causes  of  action  under  the  federal 
25  Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act (“CERCLA”), 
26                                                                            
27                                                                            
28                                                                            
1  one cause of action under California’s Hazardous Substances Account Act (“HSAA”), and 
2  nine additional tort and equitable causes of action under California state common law.  
3  (SAC ¶¶ 47–122.)  Each cause of action is premised on the alleged contamination of 
4  Plaintiff’s 1680 Property with PCE.  (Id.)                                
5       On April 27, 2023, the Kims answered Plaintiff’s SAC, denying all liability.  (Doc. 
6  155 at 1–17.)  The Kims also filed their Second Amended Third-Party Claims against 
7  M&E, the Barawids, the Hortmans, and other former owners and operators of the dry-
8  cleaning businesses previously located at the 1718 Property.  (Id. at 17–27.)  The Kims 
9  allege that the sole source of the PCE contamination is the 1718 Property, not their 1654 
10  Property.  (Id. at 18–19.)  Therefore, the Kims assert that they are entitled to contribution 
11  and/or indemnity under CERCLA, HSAA, and California Civil Code section 1432 from 
12  M&E, the Barawids, the Hortmans, and/or other former owners and operators of the dry-
13  cleaning businesses previously located at the 1718 Property.  (Id. at 20–25.)  The Kims 
14  also contend that M&E, the Barawids, the Hortmans, and the other prior owners and 
15  operators of the 1718 Property are the sole source of the contamination on the Kims’ 1654 
16  Property and are liable for those response costs as well.  (Doc. 157 at 28–30.)  On May 18, 
17  2023, M&E and the Barawids answered the Kim’s Second Amended Third-Party Claims, 
18  denying all liability.  (Doc. 128.)  Notably, M&E and the Barawids did not assert any claims 
19  against the Kims.  (Id.)                                                  
20       On May 19, 2023, the Hortmans answered Plaintiff’s SAC, denying all liability.  
21  (Doc.  129.)    Additionally,  the  Hortmans  filed  crossclaims  for  contribution  and/or 
22  indemnity under CERCLA, HSAA, and California Civil Code section 1432 against all 
23  other defendants named in Plaintiff’s SAC, including the Kims and M&E, for any potential 
24  liability to Plaintiff.  (Id. at 32.)  The Hortmans also filed a Third-Complaint Complaint 
25  against prior owners and operators of the 1718 Property dating back to the 1960s for 
26  contribution and/or indemnity under CERCLA, HSAA, and California Civil Code section 
27  1432.  (Id. at 48–63.)  These third-party defendants have not appeared in this litigation. 
28       On November 30, 2022, M&E filed a separate complaint against the Hortmans (22-
1  cv-01892-RBM-DEB, Doc. 1), which it then amended on March 22, 2023 (22-cv-01892-
2  RBM-DEB, Doc. 13).  In its First Amended Complaint against the Hortmans, M&E 
3  contends that it is entitled to the recovery of response costs and contribution for the 
4  investigation and cleanup of its 1718 Property (id. at 12–15, 23), as well as damages for 
5  negligence, nuisance, trespass, and waste (id. at 16–24).                 
6  C.   The Tentative Settlement Agreement.                                  
7       Plaintiff and M&E have reached a tentative settlement agreement.  (Doc 147-2 at 2 
8  (“Settlement Agreement”).)  The settlement agreement includes the following material 
9  terms:                                                                    
10       •  M&E  shall  deliver  to  Plaintiff’s  counsel  the  sum  of  $25,000.  (Settlement 
11         Agreement at 3.)                                                   
12       •  “This Agreement is subject to, and expressly contingent upon, a determination 
13         that the settlement contemplated by this Agreement is a good faith settlement 
14         pursuant to California Code Civil Procedure § 877.6 and various 9th Circuit case 
15         law as they pertain to CERCLA liability….”  (Id.)                  
16       •  “[I]n the alternative, entry of an order dismissing all of Pacific’s claims in the 
17         action with prejudice against all Defendants.”  (Id.)              
18  Plaintiff and M&E executed the settlement agreement on July 10, 2023.  (Id. at 7.)  
19  D.   M&E’s Motion                                                         
20       In accordance with the material terms outlined above, on July 21, 2023, M&E filed 
21  the present Motion.  (Doc. 147.)  In its Motion, M&E requests a determination that the 
22  tentative settlement agreement between M&E and Plaintiff has been made in good faith 
23  within the meaning of California Code of Civil Procedure sections 877 and 877.6 and that 
24  the  tentative  settlement  will  bar  all  existing  and/or  future  claims  against  M&E  for 
25  indemnity and/or contribution, equitable partial, or total.  (Id. at 2.)  M&E’s Motion is made 
26  on the grounds that the agreed-to settlement meets the test for good faith set forth in Tech-
27  Bilt, Inc. v. Woodward-Clyde & Associates, 38 Cal.3d 488 (1985).  (Id.)  Additionally, 
28  M&E asserts that the agreed-to settlement is fair, reasonable, and consistent with the 
1  objectives and policy underlying CERCLA, which also permits contribution protection for 
2  M&E.  (Id. at 19.)                                                        
3       Specifically, M&E argues that the proposed settlement agreement meets the test for 
4  good faith set forth in Tech-Bilt, Inc. because it is the result of lengthy, arms-length, court-
5  assisted settlement negotiations based on the information available to the parties at the time 
6  of settlement, including numerous documents and expert opinions.  (Id. at 18–19.)  M&E 
7  also contends that the non-settling defendants were provided ample opportunity to join the 
8  good-faith settlement agreement but chose not to (id. at 19), that it should have to pay less 
9  than if this matter were to proceed to trial (id. at 23), that it is not financially capable of 
10  litigating this matter and performing the investigation and remediation of its own property, 
11  and that there is no evidence of collusion or fraud (id. at 24).          
12       Most  importantly,  M&E  contends  that  its  proportionate  share  of  any  potential 
13  liability to Plaintiff is zero percent because it has never leased any portion of the 1718 
14  Property to a dry-cleaning business.  (Id. at 20.)  Rather, M&E uses the 1718 Property to 
15  operate an adult daycare business that does not utilize dry-cleaning chemicals.  (Id.)  
16  Alternatively, M&E argues that, even if it were somehow liable to Plaintiff, the evidence 
17  gathered to date indicates that the 1654 Property is the most likely source of the PCE 
18  contamination, not the 1718 Property (id. at 20–22), and that the Hortmans would share 
19  the bulk of any contamination attributed to the 1718 Property (id. at 8, 22).   M&E also 
20  notes that Plaintiff’s recovery is now capped because it has sold the 1680 Property.  (Id. at 
21  23.)                                                                      
22       Finally, M&E requests that the Court bar all liability for contribution or indemnity 
23  in connection with the “site” and the subject matter of this litigation.  (Id. at 24–25.)  M&E 
24  defines “site” as the 1654 Property, the 1718 Property, and the 1680 Property, collectively.  
25  (Id.  at  8.)   More  specifically,  M&E  requests  that  the Court  bar  and/or dismiss with 
26  prejudice: (1) Plaintiff’s claims against M&E, (2) the Hortmans’ cross complaint against 
27  M&E,  (3)  the  Kims’  Third-Party  Claims  for  contribution  and/or  indemnity,  and  (4) 
28  Defendant Angela Hong’s cross complaint against M&E.  (Id. at 25.)        
1       On July 25, 2023, Plaintiff joined the Settling Defendant’s Motion.  (Doc. 149.)   
2  E.   The Hortman Opposition                                               
3       In  their  opposition,  the  Hortmans  contend  that  the  contribution/indemnity  bar 
4  requested by M&E is overbroad.  (Doc. 158.)  Specifically, the Hortmans contend that 
5  M&E  seeks  to  be  discharged  from  all  liability  for  contribution  and/or  indemnity  in 
6  connection with the contamination of Plaintiff’s 1680 Property, the Kim’s 1654 Property, 
7  and M&E’s 1718 Property when the proposed settlement only contemplates damages 
8  attributable to Plaintiff’s investigation of the 1680 Property.  (Id. at 7.)  Hypothetically, 
9  this broad bar could prevent the Hortmans from seeking contribution and/or indemnity for 
10  costs associated with the investigation and/or cleanup of the Kim’s 1654 Property and/or 
11  M&E’s 1718 Property in addition to barring future claims related to Plaintiff’s 1680 
12  Property.    (Id.)    Such  a  broad  bar  would  also  prohibit  the  Hortmans  from  seeking 
13  contribution and/or indemnity for claims by the current or future owners of the 1680 
14  Property, which may incur additional investigation and/or cleanup costs.  (Id.)  Thus, the 
15  Hortmans request that the Court narrow the scope of the bar.  (Id. at 11.)       
16  F.   The Kim Opposition                                                   
17       In the Kim Opposition, the Kims argue that M&E’s Motion is unsupported by 
18  evidence, such as affidavits and declarations, demonstrating M&E’s proportionate share of 
19  any potential liability to Plaintiff.  (Doc. 157 at 11–12.)  The Kims then contend that M&E, 
20  as the current owner of the 1718 Property, could (and would) be held liable under CERCLA 
21  for the Kims’ investigation and cleanup costs related to Plaintiff’s 1680 Property as well 
22  as the Kims’ 1654 Property even though M&E has never leased the 1718 Property to a dry 
23  cleaner during its ownership of the 1718 Property.  (Id. at 17–20, 27–28.)  The Kims present 
24  scientific evidence that the 1718 Property is the sole source of the contamination and, 
25  therefore, that M&E’s share of the liability is greater than the amount of the settlement.  
26  (Id. at 20–27.)  Finally, the Kims contend that the indemnity/contribution bar requested by 
27  M&E  is  overly  broad  because  it  would  bar  the  Kims’  claims  against  M&E  for  the 
28  investigation and cleanup of the 1654 Property, as well as well as any indemnity and/or 
1  contribution claims stemming from a hypothetical future lawsuit from the current and/or 
2  future owners of the 1680 Property who are not a party to this litigation.  (Id. at 28–31.)  
3  Alternatively, the Kims request that the Court deny M&E’s Motion without prejudice to 
4  allow for discovery regarding M&E’s financial condition.  (Id. at 31.)    
5                         II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                
6  A.   Supplement Jurisdiction and Choice of Law                            
7       This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over Plaintiff’s CERCLA claims pursuant 
8  to  28  U.S.C.  §  1331  because  the  causes  of  action  alleged  herein  arise  under  the 
9  Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States, or are supplemental thereto.  State of 
10  Cal. on Behalf of California Dep’t of Health Servs. v. B & R Davis Fertilizers, Inc., 29 
11  F.3d 634 (9th Cir. 1994).  This Court has supplemental jurisdiction over Plaintiff’s state 
12  law claims pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367 because these claims arise out of the same nucleus 
13  of operative facts as Plaintiff’s federal CERCLA claims.  (Id.)           
14       “When  a  district  court  sits  in  diversity,  or  hears  state  law  claims  based  on 
15  supplemental jurisdiction, the court applies state substantive law to the state law claims.”  
16  Mason & Dixon Intermodal, Inc. v. Lapmaster Int’l LLC, 632 F.3d 1056, 1060 (9th Cir. 
17  2011).  The Ninth Circuit has held that California Code of Civil Procedure section 877 
18  constitutes substantive law and, therefore, that federal courts look to California law to 
19  decide whether a settlement was made in good faith with respect to the state law tort claims.  
20  Id. (citing Fed. Savings & Loan Ins. Corp. v. Butler, 904 F.2d 505, 511 (9th Cir.1990)).  
21  Although California Code of Civil Procedure section 877.6 is the procedural mechanism 
22  for section 877, “the case law is clear that state settlement provisions amount to substantive, 
23  rather than purely procedural, law.”  Slaven v. BP Am., Inc., 958 F. Supp. 1472, 1477–78 
24  (C.D. Cal. 1997).                                                         
25  B.   California Code of Civil Procedure Sections 877 and 877.7            
26       Plaintiff and M&E seek a determination that the proposed settlement has been made 
27  in good faith pursuant to California Code of Civil Procedure sections 877 and 877.6.  These 
28                                                                            
1  provisions apply to Plaintiff’s state law claims.  Mason & Dixon Intermodal, Inc., 632 F.3d 
2  at 1060; Slaven, 958 F. Supp. at 1477–78.                                 
3       Section 877 governs the effect of a release of claims given “in good faith before 
4  verdict or judgment to one or more of a number of tortfeasors claimed to be liable for the 
5  same tort, or to one or more other co-obligors mutually subject to contribution rights.”  Cal. 
6  Civ. Proc. Code § 877.  The good faith settlement “shall not discharge any other such party 
7  from liability unless its terms so provide, but it shall reduce the claims against the others 
8  in the amount stipulated by the release….”  § 877(a).  Further, “[i]t shall discharge the party 
9  to whom it is given from all liability for any contribution to any other parties.”  § 877(b).   
10       “[A] settling party may give notice of settlement to all parties and to the court, 
11  together with an application for determination of good faith settlement and a proposed 
12  order.  The application shall indicate the settling parties, and the basis, terms, and amount 
13  of the settlement.”  § 877.6(a). “A determination by the court that the settlement was made 
14  in good faith shall bar any other joint tortfeasor or co-obligor from any further claims 
15  against the settling tortfeasor or co-obligor for equitable comparative contribution, or 
16  partial or comparative indemnity, based on comparative negligence or comparative fault.”  
17  § 877.6(c).                                                               
18       In other words, “[s]ection 877 establishes that a good faith settlement bars other 
19  defendants from seeking contribution from the settling defendant, but at the same time 
20  provides that the plaintiff’s claims against the other defendants are to be reduced by the 
21  amount of consideration paid for the settlement.  Thus, while a good faith settlement cuts 
22  off the right of other defendants to seek contribution or comparative indemnity from the 
23  settling defendant, the non-settling defendants obtain in return a reduction in their ultimate 
24  liability to the plaintiff.”  Abbott Ford, Inc. v. Superior Ct., 43 Cal. 3d 858, 871–73 (1987) 
25  (citations  and  quotations  omitted).    “[T]he  provisions  of  sections  877  and  877.6—
26  governing the effect that a settlement agreement has on a settling defendant’s potential 
27  liability to other defendants for contribution or comparative indemnity—have two major 
28                                                                            
1  goals: the equitable sharing of costs among the parties at fault and the encouragement of 
2  settlements.”  Id. at 871–72.                                             
3       “The issue of the good faith of a settlement may be determined by the court on the 
4  basis of affidavits served with the notice of hearing, and any counteraffidavits filed in 
5  response….”  Id. at § 877.6(b).  To determine whether a settlement had been made in good 
6  faith, and therefore bars all future claims by any tortfeasor for contribution or indemnity, 
7  California courts consider the factors identified by the California Supreme Court in Tech-
8  Bilt, Inc.:                                                               
9       [T]he intent and policies underlying section 877.6 require that a number of 
        factors  be  taken  into  account  including  [1]  a  rough  approximation  of 
10                                                                            
        plaintiffs’  total  recovery  and  the  settlor’s  proportionate  liability,  [2]  the 
11       amount paid in settlement, [3] the allocation of settlement proceeds among 
        plaintiffs, and [4] a recognition that a settlor should pay less in settlement than 
12                                                                            
        he would if he were found liable after a trial.  Other relevant considerations 
13       include [5] the financial conditions and insurance policy limits of settling 
        defendants, as well as [6] the existence of collusion, fraud, or tortious conduct 
14                                                                            
        aimed to injure the interests of nonsettling defendants.             
15                                                                            
16  Tech-Bilt,  Inc.  v.  Woodward-Clyde  &  Assocs.,  38  Cal.  3d  488,  499–500  (1985).  
17  “[P]ractical considerations obviously require that the evaluation be made on the basis of 
18  information available at the time of settlement.”  Id.                    
19       Further, “[t]he party asserting the lack of good faith shall have the burden of proof 
20  on that issue.”  § 877.6(d).  The non-settling party is “permitted to demonstrate, if he can, 
21  that the settlement is so far ‘out of the ballpark’ in relation to these factors as to be 
22  inconsistent with the equitable objectives of the statute.”  Tech-Bilt, Inc., 38 Cal. 3d at 499–
23  500 (citations omitted).  “If contested, declarations by the non-settlor should be filed which 
24  in many cases could require the moving party to file responsive counter declarations to 
25  negate the lack of good faith asserted by the non-settling contesting party.”  City of Grand 
26  Terrace v. Superior Ct., 192 Cal. App. 3d 1251, 1261–62 (Ct. App. 1987) (emphasis 
27  added).

20  C.   CERCLA                                                               
21       M&E also seeks approval of its settlement agreement and an order providing it with 
22  contribution protection under CERCLA.  42 U.S.C. § 9613(f).  In considering this request, 
23  the Court first reviews CERCLA’s statutory framework.                     
24       Congress enacted CERCLA “in response to the serious environmental and health 
25  risks posed by industrial pollution.”  Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. United States, 
26  556  U.S.  599,  602  (2009).    CERCLA  “imposes  strict  liability  on  four  categories  of 
27  potentially responsible parties (PRPs) for the cleanup costs of an environmental hazard, 
28  even if the person did not contribute to the contamination.”  Chubb Custom Ins. Co. v. 
1  Space Sys./Loral, Inc., 710 F.3d 946, 956 (9th Cir. 2013) (emphasis added).  “CERCLA 
2  liability is joint and several, meaning that a responsible party may be held liable for the 
3  entire cost of cleanup even where other parties contributed to the contamination.  The party 
4  saddled with the cleanup costs may, in turn, sue other potentially responsible parties for 
5  contribution.”  California Dep’t of Toxic Substances Control v. Hearthside Residential 
6  Corp., 613 F.3d 910, 912 (9th Cir. 2010); see also AmeriPride Servs. Inc. v. Tex. E. 
7  Overseas  Inc.,  782  F.3d  474,  480  (9th  Cir.  2015);  42  U.S.C.  §  9607(a);  42  U.S.C. 
8  9613(f)(1).                                                               
9       There are four categories of potentially responsible parties (“PRPs”):  
10       …(1) the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility,[2] (2) any person who at 
        the time of disposal of any hazardous substance owned or operated any facility 
11                                                                            
        at which such hazardous substances were disposed of, (3) any person who by 
12       contract, agreement, or otherwise arranged for disposal or treatment … of 
        hazardous substances … , and (4) any person who accepts or accepted any 
13                                                                            
        hazardous substances for transport to disposal or treatment facilities … from 
14       which there is a release, or a threatened release which causes the incurrence 
        of response costs, of a hazardous substance…                         
15                                                                            

16  42 U.S.C. § 9607.  PRPs are responsible for “(A) all costs of removal or remedial action 
17  incurred by the United States Government or a State or an Indian tribe...; (B) any other 
18  necessary costs of response incurred by any other person…; (C) damages for injury to, 
19  destruction of, or loss of natural resources, including the reasonable costs of assessing such 
20  injury, destruction, or loss resulting from such a release; and (D) the costs of any health 
21  assessment or health effects study….”  42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(4)(A)–(D).     
22       CERCLA’s  otherwise  harsh,  strict-liability  scheme  encourages  settlement  by 
23  providing so-called “contribution protection” to “[a] person who has resolved its liability 
24  to the United States or a State in an administrative or judicially approved settlement[.]”  42 
25                                                                            

26                                                                            
27  2 “The term ‘facility’ means … any site or area where a hazardous substance has been 
   deposited, stored, disposed of, or placed, or otherwise come to be located… .”  42 U.S.C. 
28                                                                            
1  U.S.C. § 9613(f)(2).  In other words, CERCLA prevents parties settling with the United 
2  States or a State from later being sued for contribution by non-settling parties.  Id.  “Such 
3  settlement does not discharge any of the other potentially liable persons unless its terms so 
4  provide, but it reduces the potential liability of the others by the amount of the settlement.”  
5  Id.  CERCLA is silent as to whether contribution protection and the reduction of the 
6  remaining liability applies to settlement agreements between private parties.  
7       In the absence of express authority, the Ninth Circuit looks to another CERCLA 
8  provision  for  the  authority  to  allocate  costs  and  afford  contribution  protection  in 
9  settlements between private parties:  “In  resolving  contribution  claims,  the  court may 
10  allocate response costs among liable parties using such equitable factors as the court 
11  determines are appropriate.”  42 U.S.C. § 9613(f)(1) (emphasis added).  In AmeriPride 
12  Services, Inc., the Ninth  Circuit held  that  “a  district  court has discretion under  [this 
13  provision] to determine the most equitable method of accounting for settlements between 
14  private parties in a contribution action.”  782 F.3d at 487.  However, district courts must 
15  exercise their discretion in a manner that is consistent with the principles and purposes of 
16  CERCLA.  Id. at 488.  “Choosing a method that would discourage settlement or produce 
17  plainly inequitable results could constitute an abuse of discretion.”  Id.   
18       When considering the equitable allocation of costs, courts weigh the so-called “Gore 
19  Factors.”  They are “(1) the ability of the parties to demonstrate that their contribution to a 
20  discharge, release or disposal of a hazardous waste can be distinguished; (2) the amount of 
21  the hazardous waste involved; (3) the degree of toxicity of the hazardous waste involved; 
22  (4) the degree of involvement by the parties in the generation, transportation, treatment, 
23  storage, or disposal of the hazardous waste; (5) the degree of care exercised by the parties 
24  with respect to the hazardous waste concerned, taking into account the characteristics of 
25  such hazardous waste; and (6) the degree of cooperation by the parties with Federal, State, 
26  or local officials to prevent any harm to the public health or the environment.”  TDY 
27  Holdings, LLC v. United States, 885 F.3d 1142, 1146, n. 1 (9th Cir. 2018) (internal 
28  quotation omitted).                                                       
1       While districts courts are free to grant settling parties contribution protection, the 
2  scope of permissible contribution protection is limited.  “CERCLA’s policy of encouraging 
3  settlements  by  authorizing  contribution  protection  to  settling  parties  should  not  be 
4  construed in a manner that ambushes persons…who had no connection with, and no 
5  responsibility for, the pollution on the site at issue in the settlement….”  City of Emeryville 
6  v. Robinson, 621 F.3d 1251, 1264 (9th Cir. 2010).  “[T]he overwhelming majority of courts 
7  that have imposed or enforced a CERCLA contribution bar in a private-party settlement 
8  have done so only where the persons subject to the bar were either parties to the action, 
9  PRPs  who  were  involved  in  or  aware  of  settlement  discussions,  or  non-parties  who 
10  otherwise  had  at  least  constructive  notice  that  their  contribution  claims  stood  to  be 
11  extinguished.”  Id. at 1265.  A contribution bar should not extend beyond “matter expressly 
12  contemplated by the parties in entering into the [] [s]ettlement.”  Id. at 1264.

14       1.   The Equitable Allocation of Costs                               
15       As stated above, the Ninth Circuit has held that “a district court has discretion under 
16  § 9613(f)(1) to determine the most equitable method of accounting for settlements between 
17  private parties in a contribution action.”  AmeriPride Servs. Inc., 782 F.3d 474 at 487.  
18  However, district courts must exercise their discretion in a manner that is consistent with 
19  the principles and purposes of CERCLA.  Id. at 488.  “Choosing a method that would 
20  discourage settlement or produce plainly inequitable results could constitute an abuse of 
21  discretion.”  Id.                                                         
22       District  courts  also  weigh  the  “Gore  Factors”  when  considering  the  equitable 
23  allocation of costs.  The “Gore Factors” applicable to the present case are the parties’ 
24  contribution and involvement in the generation, treatment, storage, or disposal of the 
25  hazardous waste  and  the degree of care exercised  by the parties with  respect  to the 
26  hazardous waste concerned.  TDY Holdings, LLC, 885 F.3d 1142 at 1146, n. 1. 
27       For the same reasons discussed at length above (see III.A.1), the Court determines 
28  that the proposed settlement agreement is an equitable allocation of costs based on the 
1  information available to the court at this time.  Here, M&E has agreed to pay $25,000, 
2  approximately 13.5% percent, of Plaintiff’s total recovery (Doc. 147-2 at 3) even though it 
3  has never operated a polluting dry-cleaning business at the 1718 Property (Doc. 147 at 20).  
4  In other words, applying the Gore Factors, M&E’s contribution and involvement in the 
5  generation, treatment, storage, or disposal of the hazardous waste is zero, and M&E has 
6  exercised care by not polluting its property and others with toxic dry-cleaning chemicals.  
7  It is therefore within the Court’s discretion to approve M&E’s $25,000 settlement. 
8       Nevertheless, the Kims argue adamantly that M&E is strictly liable for the pollution 
9  under CERCLA as the current owner of the 1718 Property.  (Doc. 157 at 20-27.)  The Kims 
10  present scientific evidence (an expert report) that the 1718 Property is the sole source of 
11  the contamination and, therefore, that M&E’s share of the liability is greater than the 
12  amount of the settlement.  (Id.)  While the Court agrees that a current landowner can be 
13  held strictly liable for past pollution emanating from its property, the Court need not decide 
14  the merits of Plaintiff’s CERCLA claims at this juncture.  It is within the Court’s discretion 
15  to allocate settlement costs as it sees fit.  42 U.S.C. § 9613(f)(1); AmeriPride Services, Inc., 
16  782 F.3d at 487.                                                          
17       Here, M&E is contributing $25,000 for pollution that the parties agree it did not 
18  cause.  Thus, the Court finds that the contemplated settlement is fair and reasonable under 
19  CERCLA.

21       M&E also seeks approval of its settlement agreement and an order providing it with

23  the Court first reviews CERCLA’s statutory framework.                     
24       Congress enacted CERCLA “in response to the serious environmental and health 
25  risks posed by industrial pollution.”  Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. United States, 
26
556 U.S. 599, 602
  (2009).    CERCLA  “imposes  strict  liability  on  four  categories  of 
27  potentially responsible parties (PRPs) for the cleanup costs of an environmental hazard, 
28  even if the person did not contribute to the contamination.”  Chubb Custom Ins. Co. v. 
1  Space Sys./Loral, Inc.,
710 F.3d 946, 956
 (9th Cir. 2013) (emphasis added).  “CERCLA 
2  liability is joint and several, meaning that a responsible party may be held liable for the 
3  entire cost of cleanup even where other parties contributed to the contamination.  The party 
4  saddled with the cleanup costs may, in turn, sue other potentially responsible parties for 
5  contribution.”  California Dep’t of Toxic Substances Control v. Hearthside Residential 
6  Corp.,
613 F.3d 910, 912
 (9th Cir. 2010); see also AmeriPride Servs. Inc. v. Tex. E. 
7  Overseas  Inc.,
782 F.3d 474, 480
  (9th  Cir.  2015);
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a);  42  U.S.C. 
8  9613(f)(1).                                                               
9       There are four categories of potentially responsible parties (“PRPs”):  
10       …(1) the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility,[2] (2) any person who at 
        the time of disposal of any hazardous substance owned or operated any facility 
11                                                                            
        at which such hazardous substances were disposed of, (3) any person who by 
12       contract, agreement, or otherwise arranged for disposal or treatment … of 
        hazardous substances … , and (4) any person who accepts or accepted any 
13                                                                            
        hazardous substances for transport to disposal or treatment facilities … from 
14       which there is a release, or a threatened release which causes the incurrence 
        of response costs, of a hazardous substance…                         
15                                                                            

16
42 U.S.C. § 9607
.  PRPs are responsible for “(A) all costs of removal or remedial action 
17  incurred by the United States Government or a State or an Indian tribe...; (B) any other 
18  necessary costs of response incurred by any other person…; (C) damages for injury to, 
19  destruction of, or loss of natural resources, including the reasonable costs of assessing such 
20  injury, destruction, or loss resulting from such a release; and (D) the costs of any health 
21  assessment or health effects study….”
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)(4)(A)–(D).     
22       CERCLA’s  otherwise  harsh,  strict-liability  scheme  encourages  settlement  by 
23  providing so-called “contribution protection” to “[a] person who has resolved its liability 
24  to the United States or a State in an administrative or judicially approved settlement[.]”  42 
25                                                                            

26                                                                            
27  2 “The term ‘facility’ means … any site or area where a hazardous substance has been 
   deposited, stored, disposed of, or placed, or otherwise come to be located… .”  42 U.S.C. 
28
1 U.S.C. § 9613
(f)(2).  In other words, CERCLA prevents parties settling with the United 
2  States or a State from later being sued for contribution by non-settling parties.
Id.
  “Such 
3  settlement does not discharge any of the other potentially liable persons unless its terms so 
4  provide, but it reduces the potential liability of the others by the amount of the settlement.”  
5
Id.
  CERCLA is silent as to whether contribution protection and the reduction of the 
6  remaining liability applies to settlement agreements between private parties.  
7       In the absence of express authority, the Ninth Circuit looks to another CERCLA 
8  provision  for  the  authority  to  allocate  costs  and  afford  contribution  protection  in 
9  settlements between private parties:  “In  resolving  contribution  claims,  the  court may 
10  allocate response costs among liable parties using such equitable factors as the court 
11  determines are appropriate.”
42 U.S.C. § 9613
(f)(1) (emphasis added).  In AmeriPride 
12  Services, Inc., the Ninth  Circuit held  that  “a  district  court has discretion under  [this 
13  provision] to determine the most equitable method of accounting for settlements between 
14  private parties in a contribution action.”
782 F.3d at 487
.  However, district courts must 
15  exercise their discretion in a manner that is consistent with the principles and purposes of 
16  CERCLA.
Id. at 488
.  “Choosing a method that would discourage settlement or produce 
17  plainly inequitable results could constitute an abuse of discretion.”
Id.
   
18       When considering the equitable allocation of costs, courts weigh the so-called “Gore 
19  Factors.”  They are “(1) the ability of the parties to demonstrate that their contribution to a 
20  discharge, release or disposal of a hazardous waste can be distinguished; (2) the amount of 
21  the hazardous waste involved; (3) the degree of toxicity of the hazardous waste involved; 
22  (4) the degree of involvement by the parties in the generation, transportation, treatment, 
23  storage, or disposal of the hazardous waste; (5) the degree of care exercised by the parties 
24  with respect to the hazardous waste concerned, taking into account the characteristics of 
25  such hazardous waste; and (6) the degree of cooperation by the parties with Federal, State, 
26  or local officials to prevent any harm to the public health or the environment.”  TDY 
27  Holdings, LLC v. United States,
885 F.3d 1142, 1146, n. 1
 (9th Cir. 2018) (internal 
28  quotation omitted).                                                       
1       While districts courts are free to grant settling parties contribution protection, the 
2  scope of permissible contribution protection is limited.  “CERCLA’s policy of encouraging 
3  settlements  by  authorizing  contribution  protection  to  settling  parties  should  not  be 
4  construed in a manner that ambushes persons…who had no connection with, and no 
5  responsibility for, the pollution on the site at issue in the settlement….”  City of Emeryville 
6  v. Robinson,
621 F.3d 1251, 1264
 (9th Cir. 2010).  “[T]he overwhelming majority of courts 
7  that have imposed or enforced a CERCLA contribution bar in a private-party settlement 
8  have done so only where the persons subject to the bar were either parties to the action, 
9  PRPs  who  were  involved  in  or  aware  of  settlement  discussions,  or  non-parties  who 
10  otherwise  had  at  least  constructive  notice  that  their  contribution  claims  stood  to  be 
11  extinguished.”
Id. at 1265
.  A contribution bar should not extend beyond “matter expressly 
12  contemplated by the parties in entering into the [] [s]ettlement.”
Id. at 1264
.

14  A.   The Proposed Settlement Agreement is a Good Faith Settlement Agreement 
15  Pursuant  to California  Code  of  Civil Procedure  Section 877 and 877.6,  Barring 
16  Certain Claims for Indemnity and/or Contribution Against M&E              
17       1.   The Tech-Bilt, Inc. Factors                                     
18       To prevail, the Hortmans and the Kims must prove that the proposed settlement 
19  agreement is not a “good faith settlement” under California Code of Civil Procedure 
20  sections 877 and 877.6.  Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §877.6(d); see also Tech-Bilt, Inc.,
38 Cal. 21
  3d 488 at 499–500.  They have not met this burden.  A careful review of M&E’s Motion, 
22  the Hortman Opposition, the Kim Opposition, the Hortman Reply, the Kim Reply, and the 
23  operative pleadings reveals that the proposed settlement agreement satisfies the test for a 
24  good faith settlement set forth in Tech-Bilt, Inc.                        
25            a)   M&E’s Proportionate Liability                              
26       The first four Tech-Bilt, Inc. factors are the most important.  They are “[1] a rough 
27  approximation of plaintiffs’ total recovery and the settlor’s proportionate liability, [2] the 
28  amount paid in settlement, [3] the allocation of settlement proceeds among plaintiffs, and 
1  [4] a recognition that a settlor should pay less in settlement than he would if he were found 
2  liable after a trial.”  Tech-Bilt, Inc., 38 Cal. 3d at 499–500.           
3       A rough approximation of Plaintiff’s total recovery is $185,000 in response costs to 
4  retain experts to investigate the contamination and to work with the Regional Water Quality 
5  Control Board because Plaintiff no longer owns the 1680 Property and, therefore, will not 
6  continue to incur response costs.  (Doc. 138 at 2; SAC ¶ 33.)  M&E has agreed to pay 
7  $25,000,  approximately  13.5%  percent,  of  Plaintiff’s  total  recovery.    (Settlement 
8  Agreement at 3.)  The Court is persuaded that this allocation is fair based on the evidence 
9  presented by M&E in support of their Motion, as well as the evidence presented by the 
10  Kims in support of their opposition.                                      
11       M&E contends, and the Kims do not dispute, that it has never operated a dry-
12  cleaning business at the 1718 Property.  (Doc. 147 at 20.)  Instead, M&E operates an adult 
13  daycare facility that does not release any dry-cleaning chemicals into the environment.  
14  (Id.)  Nevertheless, the Kims argue adamantly that M&E is strictly liable for the pollution 
15  at all three properties.  (Doc. 157 at 20–27.)  While this may be true under CERCLA 
16  (discussed further below), the Kims have not argued or cited any law suggesting that M&E 
17  can be held strictly liable under Plaintiff’s state common law and HSAA claims.   
18       Further, even assuming that the Kims are correct, and that the sole source of the PCE 
19  contamination at all three properties is the dry cleaner previously located on M&E’s 1718 
20  Property, M&E’s proportionate share of liability is still diluted by the Hortmans’ share of 
21  liability, as well as by the shares of other prior owners and operators of the 1718 Property 
22  dating back to the 1960s.  The Kims themselves presented evidence that the dry-cleaning 
23  business located at the 1718 Property was cited for spilling chemicals during the Hortmans’ 
24  ownership,  not  M&E’s  ownership.    (Doc.  157-2  at  58.)    Thus,  the  Kims  have  not 
25  demonstrated that the settlement is “so far ‘out of the ballpark’ in relation to these factors 
26  as to be inconsistent with the equitable objectives of the statute[,]” especially considering 
27  the notion that a settling defendant should pay less that it would if found liable at trial.

12  under CERCLA, Barring Certain Claims for Indemnity and/or Contribution Against

14       1.   The Equitable Allocation of Costs                               
15       As stated above, the Ninth Circuit has held that “a district court has discretion under 
16  § 9613(f)(1) to determine the most equitable method of accounting for settlements between 
17  private parties in a contribution action.”  AmeriPride Servs. Inc.,
782 F.3d 474 at 487
.  
18  However, district courts must exercise their discretion in a manner that is consistent with 
19  the principles and purposes of CERCLA.
Id. at 488
.  “Choosing a method that would 
20  discourage settlement or produce plainly inequitable results could constitute an abuse of 
21  discretion.”
Id.
                                                         
22       District  courts  also  weigh  the  “Gore  Factors”  when  considering  the  equitable 
23  allocation of costs.  The “Gore Factors” applicable to the present case are the parties’ 
24  contribution and involvement in the generation, treatment, storage, or disposal of the 
25  hazardous waste  and  the degree of care exercised  by the parties with  respect  to the 
26  hazardous waste concerned.  TDY Holdings, LLC,
885 F.3d 1142 at 1146, n. 1
. 
27       For the same reasons discussed at length above (see III.A.1), the Court determines 
28  that the proposed settlement agreement is an equitable allocation of costs based on the 
1  information available to the court at this time.  Here, M&E has agreed to pay $25,000, 
2  approximately 13.5% percent, of Plaintiff’s total recovery (Doc. 147-2 at 3) even though it 
3  has never operated a polluting dry-cleaning business at the 1718 Property (Doc. 147 at 20).  
4  In other words, applying the Gore Factors, M&E’s contribution and involvement in the 
5  generation, treatment, storage, or disposal of the hazardous waste is zero, and M&E has 
6  exercised care by not polluting its property and others with toxic dry-cleaning chemicals.  
7  It is therefore within the Court’s discretion to approve M&E’s $25,000 settlement. 
8       Nevertheless, the Kims argue adamantly that M&E is strictly liable for the pollution 
9  under CERCLA as the current owner of the 1718 Property.  (Doc. 157 at 20-27.)  The Kims 
10  present scientific evidence (an expert report) that the 1718 Property is the sole source of 
11  the contamination and, therefore, that M&E’s share of the liability is greater than the 
12  amount of the settlement.  (Id.)  While the Court agrees that a current landowner can be 
13  held strictly liable for past pollution emanating from its property, the Court need not decide 
14  the merits of Plaintiff’s CERCLA claims at this juncture.  It is within the Court’s discretion 
15  to allocate settlement costs as it sees fit.
42 U.S.C. § 9613
(f)(1); AmeriPride Services, Inc.,

782 F.3d at 487

25                         II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                
26       Pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6), an action may be dismissed for failure to allege “enough 
27  facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”  Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 
28  U.S. 544, 570 (2007).  “A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual 
1  content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable 
2  for  the  misconduct  alleged.   The  plausibility  standard  is  not  akin to a 
3  probability requirement, but it asks for more than a sheer possibility that a defendant acted 
4  unlawfully.”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (internal quotation marks and 
5  citations omitted).  For purposes of ruling on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the Court “accept[s] 
6  factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe[s] the pleadings in the light most 
7  favorable to the nonmoving party.”  Manzarek v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co., 519 F.3d 
8  1025, 1031 (9th Cir. 2008).                                               
9       However, the Court is “not bound to accept as true a legal conclusion couched as a 
10  factual allegation.”  Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678 (quoting Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555).  Nor is the 
11  Court  “required  to  accept  as  true  allegations  that  contradict  exhibits  attached  to  the 
12  [c]omplaint or matters properly subject to judicial notice, or allegations that are merely 
13  conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.”  Daniels-Hall v. 
14  Nat’l Educ. Ass’n, 629 F.3d 992, 998 (9th Cir. 2010).  “In sum, for a complaint to survive 
15  a motion to dismiss, the non-conclusory factual content, and reasonable inferences from 
16  that content, must be plausibly suggestive of a claim entitling the plaintiff to relief.”  Moss 
17  v. U.S. Secret Serv., 572 F.3d 962, 969 (9th Cir. 2009) (quotation marks omitted). 
18       When a Rule 12(b)(6) motion is granted, “a district court should grant leave to amend 
19  even if no request to amend the pleading was made, unless it determines that the pleading 
20  could not possibly be cured by the allegation of other facts.”  Cook, Perkiss & Liehe v. N. 
21  Cal. Collection Serv., 911 F.2d 242, 247 (9th Cir. 1990) (citations omitted).   
22                            III.  DISCUSSION                                
23       “In order to prevail in a private action under CERCLA for response costs or natural 
24  resource damages, a plaintiff must prove the following elements, among others: (1) the site 
25  on  which  the  hazardous  substances  are  found  is  a  ‘facility’  within  the  meaning  of 
26  CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. § 9601(9); (2) a ‘release’ or ‘threatened release’ of any ‘hazardous 
27  substance’ from the facility has occurred, 42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(4); and (3) the defendant is 
28  within one of the four broad classes of ‘potentially responsible parties’ (‘PRPs’) listed in 
1  42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(1)–(4).”  Pakootas v. Teck Cominco Metals, LTD., 830 F.3d 975, 981 
2  (9th Cir. 2016) (citing 3550 Stevens Creek Assocs. v. Barclays Bank of Cal., 915 F.2d 1355, 
3  1358 (9th Cir.1990)).  Ms. Hong’s Motion to Dismiss concerns the third element—that she 
4  falls within one of the four broad classes of PRPs.                       
5       “The four PRP classes are: ‘(1) the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility, (2) 
6  any person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous substance owned or operated any 
7  facility at which such hazardous substances were disposed of, (3) any person who by 
8  contract, agreement, or otherwise arranged for disposal or treatment, or arranged with a 
9  transporter for transport for disposal or treatment, of hazardous substances owned or 
10  possessed by such person, by any other party or entity, at any facility or incineration vessel 
11  owned or operated by another party or entity and containing such hazardous substances, 
12  and (4) any person who accepts or accepted any hazardous substances for transport to 
13  disposal or treatment facilities, incineration vessels or sites selected by such person ....’”  
14  Id. at 982 (quoting 42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)).                                 
15       The first PRP class—“the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility”—refers to 
16  current owners or operators.  California Dep’t of Toxic Substances Control v. Hearthside 
17  Residential Corp., 613 F.3d 910, 912–13 (9th Cir. 2010) (citations omitted).  In contrast, 
18  the second PRP class—“any person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous substance 
19  ... operated any facility at which such hazardous substances were disposed of”—refers to 
20  prior owners and operators of the facility.  United States v. Sterling Centrecorp Inc., 977 
21  F.3d 750, 756 (9th Cir. 2020) (citation omitted).  “To sharpen the definition [of ‘operator’] 
22  for [the] purposes of CERCLA’s concern with environmental contamination, an operator 
23  must  manage,  direct,  or  conduct  operations  specifically  related  to  pollution,  that  is, 
24  operations having to do with the leakage or disposal of hazardous waste, or decisions about 
25  compliance with environmental regulations.”  United States v. Bestfoods, 524 U.S. 51, 66–
26  67 (1998).                                                                
27       Here,  the  Hortman  Parties  allege  that  Ms.  Hong  has  owned  and  operated  the 
28  drycleaning business located at the 1654 Property since approximately December 25, 2001.  
1  (Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint ¶ 14.)  The Hortman Parties also allege that Ms. 
2  Hong used PCE on the 1654 Property until 2013, before which she received notices of 
3  violation for PCE “vapor leaks” in 2003 and 2004, and a PCE “leak” in 2005.  (Id. ¶¶ 62, 
4  68.)  Ms. Hong asserts that the Hortman Parties’ use of the word “operate” in their Third-
5  Party Complaint is not sufficient to adequately allege that Ms. Hong is a member of the 
6  first PRP class—“the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility.”  In support of this 
7  argument, Ms. Hong cites only to the general proposition that the Court need not accept as 
8  true “threadbare recitals of a cause of action’s elements, supported by mere conclusory 
9  statements.”  (Doc. 223 at 15, n.4 (citing Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 663).)  The Court is not 
10  persuaded.  While the terms “operate,” “operates,” and “operator” are used and defined in 
11  the statute, they also have a factual meaning easily understood by the Court.  Therefore, 
12  the Court finds that the Hortman Parties’ allegation that Ms. Hong has owned and operated 
13  the drycleaning business located at the 1654 Property since approximately December 25, 
14  2001 is a factual allegation that is neither conclusory nor a mere recitation of CERCLA’s 
15  elements.                                                                 
16       Accordingly, the Court finds that the Hortman Parties’ allegation that Ms. Hong has 
17  owned and operated the drycleaning business since 2001, coupled with specific allegations 
18  regarding her use of PCE, are sufficient to establish that Ms. Hong was an owner or 
19  operator of the drycleaning facility at this stage.  Because Ms. Hong need only be “within 
20  one of the four broad classes of [PRPs] listed in 42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(1)–(4),” Pakootas, 
21  830 F.3d at 981 (emphasis added), the Court need not address Ms. Hong’s remaining 
22  arguments regarding her status as a “person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous 
23  substance  owned  or  operated  any  facility  at  which  such  hazardous  substances  were 
24  disposed of,” i.e., a past owner or operator.  42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(2).1

25                         II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                
26       Pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6), an action may be dismissed for failure to allege “enough 
27  facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”  Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550
28 U.S. 544
, 570 (2007).  “A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual 
1  content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable 
2  for  the  misconduct  alleged.   The  plausibility  standard  is  not  akin to a 
3  probability requirement, but it asks for more than a sheer possibility that a defendant acted 
4  unlawfully.”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678
 (2009) (internal quotation marks and 
5  citations omitted).  For purposes of ruling on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the Court “accept[s] 
6  factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe[s] the pleadings in the light most 
7  favorable to the nonmoving party.”  Manzarek v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co.,
519 F.3d 8 1025, 1031
 (9th Cir. 2008).                                               
9       However, the Court is “not bound to accept as true a legal conclusion couched as a 
10  factual allegation.”  Iqbal,
556 U.S. at 678
 (quoting Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555).  Nor is the 
11  Court  “required  to  accept  as  true  allegations  that  contradict  exhibits  attached  to  the 
12  [c]omplaint or matters properly subject to judicial notice, or allegations that are merely 
13  conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.”  Daniels-Hall v. 
14  Nat’l Educ. Ass’n,
629 F.3d 992, 998
 (9th Cir. 2010).  “In sum, for a complaint to survive 
15  a motion to dismiss, the non-conclusory factual content, and reasonable inferences from 
16  that content, must be plausibly suggestive of a claim entitling the plaintiff to relief.”  Moss 
17  v. U.S. Secret Serv.,
572 F.3d 962, 969
 (9th Cir. 2009) (quotation marks omitted). 
18       When a Rule 12(b)(6) motion is granted, “a district court should grant leave to amend 
19  even if no request to amend the pleading was made, unless it determines that the pleading 
20  could not possibly be cured by the allegation of other facts.”  Cook, Perkiss & Liehe v. N. 
21  Cal. Collection Serv.,
911 F.2d 242
, 247 (9th Cir. 1990) (citations omitted).   
22                            III.  DISCUSSION                                
23       “In order to prevail in a private action under CERCLA for response costs or natural 
24  resource damages, a plaintiff must prove the following elements, among others: (1) the site 
25  on  which  the  hazardous  substances  are  found  is  a  ‘facility’  within  the  meaning  of 
26  CERCLA,
42 U.S.C. § 9601
(9); (2) a ‘release’ or ‘threatened release’ of any ‘hazardous 
27  substance’ from the facility has occurred,
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)(4); and (3) the defendant is 
28  within one of the four broad classes of ‘potentially responsible parties’ (‘PRPs’) listed in 
1
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)(1)–(4).”  Pakootas v. Teck Cominco Metals, LTD.,
830 F.3d 975
, 981 
2  (9th Cir. 2016) (citing 3550 Stevens Creek Assocs. v. Barclays Bank of Cal.,
915 F.2d 1355
, 
3  1358 (9th Cir.1990)).  Ms. Hong’s Motion to Dismiss concerns the third element—that she 
4  falls within one of the four broad classes of PRPs.                       
5       “The four PRP classes are: ‘(1) the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility, (2) 
6  any person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous substance owned or operated any 
7  facility at which such hazardous substances were disposed of, (3) any person who by 
8  contract, agreement, or otherwise arranged for disposal or treatment, or arranged with a 
9  transporter for transport for disposal or treatment, of hazardous substances owned or 
10  possessed by such person, by any other party or entity, at any facility or incineration vessel 
11  owned or operated by another party or entity and containing such hazardous substances, 
12  and (4) any person who accepts or accepted any hazardous substances for transport to 
13  disposal or treatment facilities, incineration vessels or sites selected by such person ....’”  
14
Id.
 at 982 (quoting
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)).                                 
15       The first PRP class—“the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility”—refers to 
16  current owners or operators.  California Dep’t of Toxic Substances Control v. Hearthside 
17  Residential Corp.,
613 F.3d 910
, 912–13 (9th Cir. 2010) (citations omitted).  In contrast, 
18  the second PRP class—“any person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous substance 
19  ... operated any facility at which such hazardous substances were disposed of”—refers to 
20  prior owners and operators of the facility.  United States v. Sterling Centrecorp Inc., 977
21 F.3d 750, 756
 (9th Cir. 2020) (citation omitted).  “To sharpen the definition [of ‘operator’] 
22  for [the] purposes of CERCLA’s concern with environmental contamination, an operator 
23  must  manage,  direct,  or  conduct  operations  specifically  related  to  pollution,  that  is, 
24  operations having to do with the leakage or disposal of hazardous waste, or decisions about 
25  compliance with environmental regulations.”  United States v. Bestfoods,
524 U.S. 51
, 66–
26  67 (1998).                                                                
27       Here,  the  Hortman  Parties  allege  that  Ms.  Hong  has  owned  and  operated  the 
28  drycleaning business located at the 1654 Property since approximately December 25, 2001.  
1  (Hortman Parties’ Third-Party Complaint ¶ 14.)  The Hortman Parties also allege that Ms. 
2  Hong used PCE on the 1654 Property until 2013, before which she received notices of 
3  violation for PCE “vapor leaks” in 2003 and 2004, and a PCE “leak” in 2005.  (Id. ¶¶ 62, 
4  68.)  Ms. Hong asserts that the Hortman Parties’ use of the word “operate” in their Third-
5  Party Complaint is not sufficient to adequately allege that Ms. Hong is a member of the 
6  first PRP class—“the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility.”  In support of this 
7  argument, Ms. Hong cites only to the general proposition that the Court need not accept as 
8  true “threadbare recitals of a cause of action’s elements, supported by mere conclusory 
9  statements.”  (Doc. 223 at 15, n.4 (citing Iqbal,
556 U.S. at 663
).)  The Court is not 
10  persuaded.  While the terms “operate,” “operates,” and “operator” are used and defined in 
11  the statute, they also have a factual meaning easily understood by the Court.  Therefore, 
12  the Court finds that the Hortman Parties’ allegation that Ms. Hong has owned and operated 
13  the drycleaning business located at the 1654 Property since approximately December 25, 
14  2001 is a factual allegation that is neither conclusory nor a mere recitation of CERCLA’s 
15  elements.                                                                 
16       Accordingly, the Court finds that the Hortman Parties’ allegation that Ms. Hong has 
17  owned and operated the drycleaning business since 2001, coupled with specific allegations 
18  regarding her use of PCE, are sufficient to establish that Ms. Hong was an owner or 
19  operator of the drycleaning facility at this stage.  Because Ms. Hong need only be “within 
20  one of the four broad classes of [PRPs] listed in
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)(1)–(4),” Pakootas, 
21
830 F.3d at 981
 (emphasis added), the Court need not address Ms. Hong’s remaining 
22  arguments regarding her status as a “person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous 
23  substance  owned  or  operated  any  facility  at  which  such  hazardous  substances  were 
24  disposed of,” i.e., a past owner or operator.
42 U.S.C. § 9607
(a)(2).1

5                            II.  DISCUSSION                                 
6  A.   State Law Claims—California Code of Civil Procedure Sections 877 and 877.6 
7       Ms. Longs seeks a determination that the Settlement Agreement was made in good 
8  faith pursuant to California Code of Civil Procedure sections 877 and 877.6.  (Doc. 240 at 
9  2.)                                                                       
10       “When a district court … hears state law claims based on supplemental jurisdiction, 
11  the court applies state substantive law to the state law claims.”  Mason & Dixon Intermodal, 
12  Inc. v. Lapmaster Int’l LLC, 632 F.3d 1056, 1060 (9th Cir. 2011).  The Ninth Circuit has 
13  held that California Code of Civil Procedure section 877 constitutes substantive law and, 
14  therefore, that federal courts look to California law to decide whether a settlement was 
15  made in good faith with respect to state law claims.  Id. (citing Fed. Savings & Loan Ins. 
16  Corp. v. Butler, 904 F.2d 505, 511 (9th Cir.1990)); see also Slaven v. BP Am., Inc., 958 F. 
17  Supp. 1472, 1477–78 (C.D. Cal. 1997) (finding that, while California Code of Civil 
18  Procedure section 877.6 is the procedural mechanism for section 877, “the case law is clear 
19  that  state  settlement  provisions  amount to substantive,  rather  than purely  procedural, 
20  law.”).                                                                   
21       California Code of Civil Procedure section 877 governs the effect of a release of 
22  claims given “in good faith before verdict or judgment to one or more of a number of 
23  tortfeasors claimed to be liable for the same tort, or to one or more other co-obligors 
24  mutually subject to contribution rights.”  Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 877.  The good faith 
25  settlement “shall not discharge any other such party from liability unless its terms so 
26  provide, but it shall reduce the claims against the others in the amount stipulated by the 
27  release … .”  Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 877(a).  Further, “[i]t shall discharge the party to 
28  whom it is given from all liability for any contribution to any other parties.”  Cal. Civ. Proc. 
1  Code  § 877(b).    Determinations  of  good  faith  made  under  California  Code  of  Civil 
2  Procedure sections 877 and 877.6 apply to claims asserted under the HSAA in addition to 
3  California state common law tort claims.  Fullerton Redevelopment Agency v. S. Cal. Gas 
4  Co., 183 Cal. App. 4th 428, 432 (2010).                                   
5       “[A] settling party may give notice of settlement to all parties and to the court, 
6  together with an application for determination of good faith settlement and a proposed 
7  order.  The application shall indicate the settling parties, and the basis, terms, and amount 
8  of the settlement.”  Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 877.6(a).  “A determination by the court that the 
9  settlement was made in good faith shall bar any other joint tortfeasor or co-obligor from 
10  any further claims against the settling tortfeasor or co-obligor for equitable comparative 
11  contribution, or partial or comparative indemnity, based on comparative negligence or 
12  comparative fault.”  Id. § 877.6(c).  In other words, “[s]ection 877 establishes that a good 
13  faith  settlement  bars  other  defendants  from  seeking  contribution  from  the  settling 
14  defendant, but at the same time provides that the  plaintiff’s claims against the other 
15  defendants are to be reduced by the amount of consideration paid for the settlement.  Thus, 
16  while a good faith settlement cuts off the right of other defendants to seek contribution or 
17  comparative indemnity from the settling defendant, the non-settling defendants obtain in 
18  return a reduction in their ultimate liability to the plaintiff.”  Abbott Ford, Inc. v. Superior 
19  Ct., 43 Cal. 3d 858, 872–73 (1987) (citations and quotations omitted).  “[T]he provisions 
20  of sections 877 and 877.6—governing the effect that a settlement agreement has on a 
21  settling defendant’s potential liability to other defendants for contribution or comparative 
22  indemnity—have two major goals: the equitable sharing of costs among the parties at fault 
23  and the encouragement of settlements.”  Id. at 871–72.                    
24       “The issue of the good faith of a settlement may be determined by the court on the 
25  basis of affidavits served with the notice of hearing, and any counteraffidavits filed in 
26  response … .”  Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 877.6(b).  To determine whether a settlement has 
27  been  made  in  good  faith,  and  therefore  bars  all  future  claims  by  any  tortfeasor  for 
28

3  to the motion has been filed … the Tech-Bilt factors are not considered or weighed.”). 
4       Should a court grant an application for a good faith settlement determination under 
5  California Code of Civil Procedure sections 877 and 877.6, “only those non-parties with 
6  constitutionally  sufficient  prior  notice  will  be  bound  by  a  ‘good  faith  settlement’ 
7  determination[.]”  City of Emeryville v. Robinson, 621 F.3d 1251, 1266 (9th Cir. 2010) 
8  (emphasis added); Gackstetter v. Frawley, 135 Cal. App. 4th 1257, 1273 (2006) (“A 
9  settling tortfeasor’s section 877.6, subdivision (c) good faith settlement determination 
10  discharges indemnity claims by other tortfeasors, whether or not named as parties, so long 
11  as the other tortfeasors were given notice and an opportunity to be heard.”) (emphasis 
12  added).                                                                   
13       1.   Tech-Bilt, Inc. Analysis                                        
14       As the present Settlement Motion is unopposed, the Court need not weigh the Tech-
15  Bilt factors.  See Michell, 2011 WL 3903220, at *2; Hernandez, 2009 WL 322937, at *3; 
16  Bonds, 2008 WL 4104272, at *5.  Nevertheless, a careful review of the Settlement Motion 
17  and the operative pleadings reveals that the Settlement Agreement satisfies the test for a 
18  good faith settlement set forth in Tech-Bilt, Inc.                        
19       The first Tech-Bilt, Inc. factors are the most important.  Cooper Drum Cooperating 
20  Parties Grp. v. Am. Polymers Corp., Case No.: CV 19-03007-AB (FFMx), 2020 WL 
21  2504331, at *4 (C.D. Cal. May 13, 2020).  They are “[1] a rough approximation of 
22  plaintiffs’ total recovery and the settlor’s proportionate liability, [2] the amount paid in 
23  settlement, [3] the allocation of settlement proceeds among plaintiffs, and [4] a recognition 
24  that a settlor should pay less in settlement than he would if he were found liable after a 
25  trial.”  Tech-Bilt, Inc., 38 Cal. 3d at 499.  Here, William Koska, counsel for Ms. Long, 
26  declared that “[a]fter several calls and correspondence with counsel for [the Hortman 
27  Parties] over the course of July and August 2024, [Ms. Long and the Hortman Parties] have 
28  arrived at a settlement figure of $7,500.00, or one (1) percent of the total amount of 
1  estimated clean-up costs.”  (Doc. 240-1 at 2, Declaration of William K. Koska in Support 
2  of Motion for Determination of Good Faith Settlement (“Koska Decl.”), ¶ 6.)  The Court 
3  is  persuaded  that  this  amount  is  sufficient  given  Ms.  Long’s  relatively  brief  tenure 
4  operating the dry-cleaning business located at the 1654 Property.  (See Long Decl. ¶¶ 1, 4–
5  5 (declaring Ms. Long ran the dry-cleaning business for approximately 31 months from 
6  June 1999 until December 2001 when the dry-cleaning business was sold to Angela Hong, 
7  who still runs the business).)  The Court also finds that this amount is sufficient because “a 
8  settlor should pay less in settlement than [she] would if [she] were found liable after a 
9  trial.”  Tech-Bilt, Inc., 38 Cal. 3d at 499–500.                          
10       “Other relevant considerations include [5] the financial conditions and insurance 
11  policy limits of settling defendants, as well as [6] the existence of collusion, fraud, or 
12  tortious conduct aimed to injure the interests of nonsettling defendants.”  Id. at 499–500.  
13  Here, Ms. Long declared that she hopes to retire towards the end of this year and that her 
14  seamstress salary is $46,000 per year.  (Long Decl. ¶¶ 10–11.)  Ms. Long also declared 
15  that, after she retires, she will get only her Social Security benefit of approximately $2,400

17  business declined to defend her.  (Id. ¶¶ 11–12.)  Therefore, the Court finds that Ms. Long’s 
18  financial condition weighs in favor of a good faith settlement determination.  Further, there 
19  is no evidence before the Court that the proposed settlement is the result of collusion, fraud, 
20  or tortious conduct.  See Tech-Bilt, Inc., 38 Cal. 3d at 499.

3  B.   CERCLA                                                               
4       Ms. Long also seeks approval of the Settlement Agreement and an order providing 
5  her contribution protection under CERCLA.  42 U.S.C. § 9613(f).  In considering this 
6  request, the Court first reviews CERCLA’s statutory framework.            
7       Congress enacted CERCLA “in response to the serious environmental and health 
8  risks posed by industrial pollution.”  Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. United States, 
9  556  U.S.  599,  602  (2009).    CERCLA  “imposes  strict  liability  on  four  categories  of 
10  potentially responsible parties (PRPs) for the cleanup costs of an environmental hazard, 
11  even if the person did not contribute to the contamination.”  Chubb Custom Ins. Co. v. 
12  Space Sys./Loral, Inc., 710 F.3d 946, 956–57 (9th Cir. 2013) (emphasis added); see also 
13  United  States  v.  Coeur  d’Alenes  Co.,  767  F.3d  873,  874  (9th  Cir.  2014)  (CERCLA 
14  “imposes strict liability on certain classes of parties who are potentially responsible for a 
15  site’s  contamination.”)  (internal  quotation  omitted).    “CERCLA  liability  is  joint  and 
16  several, meaning that a responsible party may be held liable for the entire cost of cleanup 
17  even where other parties contributed to the contamination.  The party saddled with the 
18  cleanup costs may, in turn, sue other potentially responsible parties for contribution.”  Cal. 
19  Dep’t of Toxic Substances Control v. Hearthside Residential Corp., 613 F.3d 910, 912 (9th 
20  Cir. 2010); see also AmeriPride Servs. Inc. v. Tex. E. Overseas Inc., 782 F.3d 474, 480 (9th 
21  Cir. 2015); 42 U.S.C. § 9607(a); 42 U.S.C. § 9613(f)(1).                  
22       There are four categories of PRPs:                                   
23       (1) the owner and operator of a vessel or a facility,[4] (2) any person who at 
        the time of disposal of any hazardous substance owned or operated any facility 
24                                                                            
        at which such hazardous substances were disposed of, (3) any person who by 
25

28                                                                            
1       contract, agreement, or otherwise arranged for disposal or treatment … of 
        hazardous substances … , and (4) any person who accepts or accepted any 
2

3       which there is a release, or a threatened release which causes the incurrence 
        of response costs, of a hazardous substance…
